claims.text: Devin's PR merge rate improved from 34% to 67% over 2025, which the DeployHQ guide notes means roughly one-third of PRs still need significant rework.
Devin is reported to complete vulnerability remediation in an average of 1.5 minutes versus 30 minutes for a human developer.
Devin is reported to handle framework migrations (e.g., Angular to React, .NET Framework to .NET Core) 10-14x faster than manual effort.
Devin is reported to boost test coverage from 50-60% to 80-90% by writing missing tests.
Devin spins up its own cloud environment with a terminal, code editor, and browser, then works autonomously, delivering results as a pull request on GitHub.
Devin's workflow is: plan (shows the plan), code in its cloud IDE, run the test suite and fix failures, then push a feature branch and open a PR.
Every Devin terminal command, file edit, and browser action is recorded in a full replay timeline, and users can intervene with chat messages to redirect it.
Devin can respond to review comments and push fixes only while its session is active.
One ACU (Agent Compute Unit) is roughly 15 minutes of active Devin work, covering VM time, model inference and networking; the Teams plan's 250 ACUs equal about 62 hours of agent work per month.
Devin has read/write access to code, PRs, issues and workflows on GitHub, read-only access to deployments and security advisories, and cannot create new repositories.
Devin looks for a custom PR template at .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/devin_pr_template.md before falling back to the standard template.
Devin produces a visible multi-step written plan before touching any file, serving as a planning checkpoint where users can course-correct before execution.

A Medium explainer describes Devin's plan as better understood as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) than a numbered list, with a continuous plan-execute-observe-re-plan loop (the author's interpretation, not vendor documentation).
Cloud Devin works session-based with an Ask mode for planning and an Agent mode for autonomous execution; the Devin CLI runs the same loop locally and can hand a task off to a cloud session.
Devin automatically looks for an AGENTS.md file in the project for setup commands, code standards, test requirements and workflow; repositories must first be indexed.
Devin Knowledge stores project- or organization-wide guidance that is retrieved automatically only when relevant rather than loaded fully into every context.
Devin Playbooks bundle reusable procedures for recurring tasks and standardise recurring workflows across a team.
The Devin CLI does not yet support Knowledge, Playbooks, or Secrets from a Devin account, according to the documentation.
The Devin CLI uses an Allow/Ask/Deny permission model with an optional sandbox that restricts write access and refuses to start rather than run unsandboxed if sandbox resolution fails.
Devin does not support custom LLM API keys or model endpoints, as it is built as a closed 'compound AI system'.

Cognition's cloud execution layer gives every task a dedicated secure development environment on specialized VM infrastructure, with state persisting across steps and sessions, and an orchestration layer letting thousands of agents run concurrently.

Cognition describes Devin as the autonomous cloud agent for multi-hour tasks, and says Cognition's platform provides session timelines, audit logs with Git-linked execution lineage, and post-session analysis of credit usage and issue detection.
Windsurf was renamed Devin Desktop on June 2, 2026; its default screen became an Agent Command Center board of local and cloud agent sessions, and the local agent Devin Local replaced Cascade.
Cascade memories and workflows are not supported by Devin Local and must be migrated into skills; App Deploys and Arena mode are unavailable with Devin Local.

NewMarketPitch reports independent evidence that agents perform much better on documentation and bug fixes than on complex new features, and that a large share of agent-generated pull requests still gets rejected.
